Hosta decorata is one of the oldest named hostas in Western cultivation, prized for its blunt-tipped, dark green leaves edged in a crisp white band and for flower scapes that hold their lavender-purple blooms well above the foliage rather than nestled within it. It forms a tidy, slow-spreading clump that works well as an edging plant along shaded paths or in mixed woodland borders. Divide congested clumps in early spring or fall to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.

Hosta venusta is a true miniature species native to Jeju Island, South Korea, forming tight tufts of small, glossy, dark green leaves only a few inches tall. In late summer it sends up thin, wiry scapes bearing purple, bell-shaped flowers disproportionately large for its diminutive foliage. Its tiny stature makes it well suited to shaded rock gardens, troughs, and the front edge of a woodland bed, and it has been used extensively as breeding stock for miniature hosta hybrids.

Hosta crispula is a classic Japanese garden hosta prized for its glossy, dark green, wavy-margined leaves banded with a crisp, irregular white edge, among the earliest variegated hostas introduced to Western gardens. Clumps form an upright, vase-shaped mound and produce pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in mid to late summer. Give it consistent moisture and some protection from afternoon sun to keep leaf margins from scorching.

Hosta nakaiana is a compact Korean species with small, glossy, rounded-to-ovate green leaves and a low, dense mounding habit. It produces slender scapes of purple, bell-shaped flowers in summer, somewhat earlier than many larger hosta species bloom. Valued by collectors and hybridizers for its tidy size and glossy foliage, it suits the front of a shaded border or a woodland rock garden.

Hosta 'Tiki Bar' arose as a sport of the miniature cultivar 'Appletini' and was introduced through Bob Solberg's Green Hill Farm nursery, forming a tight, small, mounding clump of slightly folded, heart-shaped leaves with apple-green to yellow-green centers edged in a wide, darker green margin. Pale lavender flowers appear on compact scapes in summer, in proportion with its small stature. Its dense, slow-growing habit makes it well suited to container culture, rock gardens, or the front edge of a shaded perennial bed.
